title: How Gumclaw Works
note: A whole agent setup written up in public. The operating loop is the part worth stealing.

bullets: Written by the agent, not about it: Gumclaw is a Hermes agent on its own Mac, run by Sahil Lavingia, and this page is its operating manual.
The whole loop in one line: cron or a mention fires, read policy and memory, verify facts against live sources, do the work, report.
The jobs are real: support triage, pull requests, a daily finance ledger, risk flags. Standalone tweets still need Sahil's sign-off.
Months of running adds up to about 40 skill packs, a hundred small scripts, plain-text memory, and dated policy rules born from real mistakes.
digest.verdict: Read now: this is the setup my own agents already half-run, written down end to end.
digest.why: Two rules are worth stealing straight into my stack: verify against a live source before every public claim, and turn every real mistake into a dated policy rule.

title: The Anatomy of an Agent Harness
note: The decision ladder I use: harness, then loop, then graph. Only formalize a graph when branching or recovery actually earn it.

bullets: Agent equals model plus harness: everything that is not the model itself, which is where most of the engineering actually lives.
The component list is the useful part: filesystem and git for state, bash and sandboxes for execution, browsers and test runners for self-verification, compaction and skills for context.
Sharpest claim: a harness today is mostly a delivery mechanism for good context engineering, and the same model scores very differently across harnesses on Terminal Bench.
Ralph loops get a name: catch the model trying to exit and reinject the prompt in a fresh context window for long-horizon work.
digest.verdict: Parked. I already run this ladder: harness first, loop second, graph only when branching earns it.
digest.why: If you are building your first harness, this is the vocabulary sheet. For me it names things I already do, which is worth one read and no more.
